context_blurb:
Everything around you is built of atoms, each about a ten-billionth of a metre across, far too small to see inside. Yet between 1897 and 1932 a few physicists worked out what an atom holds. The parts they found decide what each element is and how it reacts.

In 1897 at Cambridge, J. J. Thomson studied cathode rays, which stream from the negative plate of a glass tube pumped almost empty of air. Charged plates bent them toward the positive side, so they were negative. A magnet bent them too, and the two bends gave their mass for each unit of charge, the same whatever gas or metal he used. Thomson concluded that the rays were negatively charged pieces of atoms, found inside every atom. He called them corpuscles; we call them electrons, each some 1,800 times lighter than a hydrogen atom.

A whole atom, though, has no charge, so something positive must balance its electrons. In 1904 Thomson pictured that positive charge spread evenly all through the atom, with the electrons set inside it. Later it was nicknamed the plum pudding. Charge spread so thin could only nudge a passing particle by a few degrees at most.

At Manchester in 1909, Hans Geiger and an undergraduate, Ernest Marsden, working for Ernest Rutherford, fired alpha particles at gold foil. An alpha particle is a helium atom that has lost both its electrons. A whole helium atom has no charge, so losing two negative electrons leaves an alpha particle with a charge of plus two. Counting the tiny sparks the particles made on a screen, in the dark, they saw most go straight through, but a very few bounce back. Rutherford later said it was as if a 15-inch artillery shell fired at tissue paper had come back and hit him.

In 1911 Rutherford worked out why. Only something very heavy and strongly charged, packed into a tiny space, could hurl an alpha particle back. So each atom has a tiny, heavy centre holding nearly all its mass: the nucleus. Most of each atom is empty space. The nucleus is less than a ten-thousandth of the atom's width, so nearly every alpha particle misses every nucleus, and the electrons it meets are far too light to turn it.

Rutherford's atom had a flaw: by the old physics, a circling electron would leak light and spiral into the nucleus in about a hundred-millionth of a second. Niels Bohr answered in 1913 with a new rule. An electron can only be at certain energy levels, like the steps of a staircase. It gives off light only when it drops to a lower level, and each drop makes one set colour, which is why glowing hydrogen shows just a few sharp colours. Physicists later swapped his neat orbits for a cloud, but kept the levels.

Until 1932 most physicists thought a nucleus held protons, its positive particles, with electrons tucked among them. In Paris, Irène Joliot-Curie and Frédéric Joliot saw a strange radiation from beryllium knock fast protons out of paraffin wax and took it for gamma rays, a powerful kind of light. At Cambridge, James Chadwick aimed it at paraffin and at several gases. Light, he showed, would need impossibly great energy to kick protons so hard, while a particle as heavy as a proton could do it easily, as one billiard ball knocks another. The radiation was a stream of neutral particles about as heavy as protons: neutrons. So a nucleus is made of protons and neutrons, and the electrons move in a cloud far outside it.

The number of protons, the atomic number, decides which element an atom is: 79 makes gold, and 82 makes lead. For centuries alchemists dreamed of making gold from lead, but to turn a lead atom into gold, three protons would have to leave its nucleus. Remove electrons and it is still lead, only charged; remove neutrons and it is lighter lead. Chemistry only shuffles electrons and never touches the nucleus, so no alchemist's furnace could ever make gold.

Electrons decide how an atom reacts. They sit in shells, and the outermost ones, the valence electrons, meet other atoms in a reaction. Sodium's eleven electrons fill shells of 2, 8 and 1; potassium's nineteen fill 2, 8, 8 and 1. Yet both have the same number of outer electrons, a single one that is easily given up, so both react fiercely with water.
